name: pair-fold
summary: Folds left over a list's PAIRS rather than its elements, handing kons each successive tail so it can see ahead and safely splice.
explanation: fold hands your procedure one element at a time, which is enough for almost everything and not enough for two things: looking ahead, and changing the list you are walking. pair-fold fixes both by handing over the pair instead of the element. At step one kons receives the whole list, at step two the list minus its head, and so on down to the last one-element tail -- so (car p) is the element fold would have given you and (cdr p) is everything still to come. That makes differences, run lengths, and lookahead comparisons natural instead of awkward. The second gift is subtler and is the reason the verb exists at all: pair-fold saves each pair's cdr BEFORE calling kons, so kons may call set-cdr! on that pair and the walk still finishes. That is what makes in-place list surgery expressible without writing the loop by hand. It is n-ary like fold, stopping at the shortest list, and left-associating: the last tail is processed last.

examples.note: ((3) (2 3) (1 2 3)) -- each step gets a whole tail, not an element, and left folding puts the last tail deepest.

examples.code:
(define (gaps xs)
  (reverse (pair-fold (lambda (p acc)
                        (if (null? (cdr p)) acc (cons (- (cadr p) (car p)) acc)))
                      '() xs)))
(display (list 'readings '(3 7 6 10) 'gaps (gaps '(3 7 6 10))))
(newline)
examples.note: (readings (3 7 6 10) gaps (4 -1 4)) -- differences between neighbours need lookahead, which is exactly what the pair gives you.

examples.code:
(define live (list 1 2 3 4 5 6))
(define anchor (cons 'anchor live))
(pair-fold (lambda (p acc)
             (let drop ()
               (if (and (pair? (cdr p)) (even? (cadr p)))
                   (begin (set-cdr! p (cddr p)) (drop))))
             acc)
           'ok anchor)
(display (list 'odds-only (cdr anchor)))
(newline)
examples.note: (odds-only (1 3 5)) -- the list is filtered in place while it is being walked, which only works because pair-fold saved each cdr first.

caveats: kons receives a PAIR, not an element. Use (car p) for the element and (cdr p) for the rest.
The last call receives the final one-element tail, whose cdr is (). Guard with (null? (cdr p)) or (pair? (cdr p)) before looking ahead.
kons may safely set-cdr! the pair it was handed -- the cdr was saved first. That is the whole point of the verb.
Splicing does NOT stop the walk. pair-fold keeps visiting nodes you have already unlinked, so a predicate that matches consecutive elements must drop them in a loop rather than one per step.
Destructive use wants an anchor pair in front of the list, because the first real node can be removed and a variable pointing at it goes stale.
It is n-ary and stops at the shortest list, like fold and map.
It requires proper lists. A dotted list raises rather than stopping at the improper tail.
It folds LEFT. For tails in front-to-back order in the result, use pair-fold-right or reverse the answer.
usecases: Computing differences, run lengths, or any comparison between neighbouring elements.
Deleting or splicing nodes out of a list in place while walking it.
Any algorithm that needs each suffix of a list rather than each element.

learn.concept: Handing a fold the pair instead of the element buys two things at once: lookahead, and the right to mutate the list you are standing on.
learn.progression: Use fold until you hit a problem that needs the next element as well as the current one, and notice how awkward it is to carry the previous value in the accumulator. Then use pair-fold and take (cadr p). Then try deleting from a list while folding over it, watch the ordinary loop lose its footing, and see why pair-fold saves the cdr first.

provenance: SRFI-1 (fold, unfold and map: pair-fold); record authored 2026-08-04

(define (gaps readings)
  (reverse (pair-fold (lambda (p acc)
                        (if (null? (cdr p)) acc (cons (- (cadr p) (car p)) acc)))

row-2-audit.math-program:
(define (inversions xs)
  (pair-fold (lambda (p acc) (+ acc (count (lambda (y) (> (car p) y)) (cdr p)))) 0 xs))
(display (list 'sorted (inversions '(1 2 3 4))
               'reversed (inversions '(4 3 2 1))
               'mixed (inversions '(2 4 1 3))))
(newline)
row-2-audit.cs-program:
(define (visited-pairs xs)
  (reverse (pair-fold (lambda (p acc) (cons p acc)) '() xs)))
(define (structure-report xs)
  (let ((ps (visited-pairs xs)))
    (list 'nodes (length ps)
          'lengths (map length ps)
          'links (let walk ((q ps) (ok 0))
                   (if (or (null? q) (null? (cdr q)))
                       ok
                       (walk (cdr q) (if (eq? (cdr (car q)) (cadr q)) (+ ok 1) ok)))))))
(display (list 'three (structure-report '(a b c))
               'one (structure-report '(z))
               'none (structure-report '())))
(newline)
row-2-audit.problem: A logger has a list of readings and must report the change between each reading and the next. Candidates: pair-fold (one traversal, and the next reading is (cadr p), sitting right there), fold carrying the previous value in the accumulator (works, but the accumulator now holds two unrelated things -- the answer being built and a scrap of walking state -- and the first step needs a sentinel that is not a reading), (map - (cdr xs) xs) (short and correct and the real competitor; it costs two traversals and a cdr allocation, and it silently answers () for a one-element list which may be what you want or may be the bug), a hand-written named let (fine, and this is exactly the loop pair-fold is), zipping the list with its own tail (the same idea with more allocation). pair-fold is the pick when the comparison is the point AND the result must know it reached the end -- and it is the only one of these that could also delete a reading on the way past.
row-2-audit.explanation: eng: gaps between neighbouring readings, over four readings, two readings, and one -- a single reading has no neighbour, so the honest answer is the empty list rather than zero. math: inversion count, which asks for every pair (i, j) with i before j and a bigger value, over a sorted list, a reversed list, and a mixed one; each suffix is exactly the set of later elements. cs: the pairs themselves, reported as a count, their lengths, and how many of them are cdr-linked to the next one visited -- which shows pair-fold hands back the list's own nodes and not copies.
row-2-audit.meta: The links count in the cs program is the check that matters: n pairs from a list of n, each one the cdr of the last. If pair-fold ever handed back a freshly consed tail the lengths would still look right and the links would drop to zero, and no test that only inspects (car p) would notice.
row-2-audit.eng: A gap list is one shorter than the reading list, always. Code that assumes they are the same length is the most common bug in this shape, and running it on a single reading is what finds it.
row-2-audit.math: Inversions count how far a permutation is from sorted, and they are exactly the number of swaps bubble sort would perform. Every suffix is the set of elements that come later, so a pair-fold is the definition transcribed.
row-2-audit.cs: A list is its pairs. pair-fold is the only fold in the library that admits this, which is why it is the one you can mutate through.

rungs.domain: a thermometer tape scanned for how long each reading keeps rising
rungs.code:
(define tape '(18 19 21 20 20 23 25 26 22))
(define (rising-runs readings)
  (reverse
   (pair-fold (lambda (p acc)
                (let walk ((q p) (n 1))
                  (if (and (pair? (cdr q)) (< (car q) (cadr q)))
                      (walk (cdr q) (+ n 1))
                      (cons (list (car p) n) acc))))
              '() readings)))
(display (list 'runs (rising-runs tape)
               'longest (apply max (map cadr (rising-runs tape)))))
(newline)

rungs.domain: a live job queue whose completed entries are unlinked in place while the queue is being walked
rungs.code:
(define (purge! head pred)
  (pair-fold (lambda (p acc)
               (let drop ()
                 (if (and (pair? (cdr p)) (pred (cadr p)))
                     (begin (set-cdr! p (cddr p)) (drop))))
               (+ acc 1))
             0 head))
(define queue (list (list 'a 'done) (list 'b 'run) (list 'c 'done) (list 'd 'wait) (list 'e 'done)))
(define anchor (cons 'anchor queue))
(define visited (purge! anchor (lambda (job) (eq? (cadr job) 'done))))
(display (list 'kept (cdr anchor) 'nodes-visited visited 'stale-head (car queue)))
(newline)

row-3-dimension.explanation: On bare numbers each tail is read once and reduced -- its length, its sum -- and nothing looks past the pair it was handed. On the thermometer tape each tail starts a second, inner walk that runs forward as far as the readings keep climbing, so the fold is now quadratic in the worst case and every step consumes an unknown amount of the future. In the job queue the fold WRITES: each step unlinks every completed entry that follows it, in a loop, and the queue changes shape underneath the walk while the walk keeps going. Same fold; what climbs is how much of the rest of the list each step touches, and finally whether it touches it read-only.
row-3-dimension.meta: The third rung shows both destructive gotchas at once. The anchor pair exists because the first real entry can be removed and nothing else would be holding the new head. nodes-visited is 6 for a five-entry queue that ends up with two entries, because pair-fold walks every node the list originally had, including the three it just unlinked -- it is following cdrs it saved, not the list as it now stands.
row-3-dimension.eng: A queue that is filtered by rebuilding it hands every other holder of that list a stale head. Unlinking in place keeps every existing reference valid, which is why long-lived structures get edited rather than replaced.
row-3-dimension.math: The longest rising run starting at each position is a classic dynamic-programming table, and computing it naively from each suffix is the honest quadratic version of it. Seeing the quadratic first is how the linear one gets earned.
row-3-dimension.cs: Saving the cdr before calling the callback is a two-line implementation detail that changes what the verb can express. It is the difference between an iterator and a cursor.

row-4-proof.eng-program:
(define (visits-every-tail? xs)
  (let ((seen (reverse (pair-fold (lambda (p acc) (cons p acc)) '() xs))))
    (and (= (length seen) (length xs))
         (let loop ((s seen) (i 0))
           (cond ((null? s) #t)
                 ((eq? (car s) (list-tail xs i)) (loop (cdr s) (+ i 1)))
                 (else #f))))))
(display (map visits-every-tail? '(() (a) (a b) (1 2 3 4 5) ((x) (y)))))
(newline)
row-4-proof.math-program:
(define (reduces-like-fold? xs)
  (and (equal? (pair-fold (lambda (p acc) (cons (car p) acc)) '() xs)
               (fold cons '() xs))
       (equal? (pair-fold-right (lambda (p acc) (cons (car p) acc)) '() xs)
               (fold-right cons '() xs))
       (equal? (pair-fold (lambda (p acc) (+ acc 1)) 0 xs) (length xs))))
(display (map reduces-like-fold? '(() (1) (1 2 3) (a b) ((1 2) (3)))))
(newline)
row-4-proof.cs-program:
(define (splice-matches-filter? xs pred)
  (let* ((pure (filter (lambda (v) (not (pred v))) xs))
         (head (cons 'h (list-copy xs))))
    (pair-fold (lambda (p acc)
                 (let drop ()
                   (if (and (pair? (cdr p)) (pred (cadr p)))
                       (begin (set-cdr! p (cddr p)) (drop))))
                 acc)
               'ok head)
    (equal? (cdr head) pure)))
(display (map (lambda (xs) (splice-matches-filter? xs even?))
              '((1 2 3 4) (2 2 2) (1 3 5) () (2) (2 1 2 2 3))))
(newline)
row-4-proof.claim: pair-fold visits exactly as many pairs as the list has elements, and the pair handed over at step i is the list's own i-th tail, not a copy; using only (car p) it computes exactly what fold computes; and unlinking nodes through the pairs it hands over produces exactly what a pure filter would have produced, including when the matching elements are adjacent.
row-4-proof.invariant: For all proper lists x: the sequence of pairs p_0..p_{n-1} passed to kons satisfies p_i eq? list-tail(x, i) and n = length(x); pair-fold(lambda (p a) (kons (car p) a), z, x) = fold(kons, z, x); and splicing out every element satisfying pred, via set-cdr! on the pairs handed over, leaves the list equal? to filter(not-pred, x)
row-4-proof.meta: Three claims: identity of the pairs, agreement with fold, and correctness of destructive splicing. What would falsify them: a tail that was freshly consed rather than the list's own node, an off-by-one that skipped the last one-element tail, or a splice that left a matching element behind. The (2 2 2) and (2 1 2 2 3) cases exist for that last one -- one splice per step is NOT enough when matches are adjacent, because the walk resumes from the saved cdr and never revisits the node it just linked past.
row-4-proof.eng: If the pairs were copies, set-cdr! through them would edit garbage and the original list would be untouched. Proving they are the list's own nodes is what licenses every destructive use of this verb.
row-4-proof.math: Restricted to (car p), pair-fold IS fold. That containment is what makes it safe to reach for the wider verb without relearning the fold's associativity or its argument order.
row-4-proof.cs: The adjacent-match case is the whole trap. A one-splice-per-step version passes every test whose matches are separated, which is most hand-written tests, and quietly leaves elements behind on real data.

row-5-emergence.eng-composition:
(define (deltas xs)
  (reverse (pair-fold (lambda (p acc)
                        (if (null? (cdr p)) acc (cons (- (cadr p) (car p)) acc)))
                      '() xs)))
(define (alarm-report xs limit)
  (let ((d (deltas xs)))
    (if (null? d)
        (list 'points (length xs) 'spikes '() 'worst 0)
        (let loop ((ds d) (i 1) (spikes '()))
          (if (null? ds)
              (list 'points (length xs) 'spikes (reverse spikes) 'worst (apply max (map abs d)))
              (loop (cdr ds) (+ i 1)
                    (if (> (abs (car ds)) limit) (cons i spikes) spikes)))))))
(display (list 'tight (alarm-report '(10 12 9 30 31) 5)
               'loose (alarm-report '(10 12 9 30 31) 25)
               'flat (alarm-report '(4) 1)))
(newline)
row-5-emergence.math-composition:
(define (suffixes xs)
  (reverse (pair-fold (lambda (p acc) (cons p acc)) '() xs)))
(define (max-gain prices)
  (let loop ((ss (suffixes prices)) (best 0))
    (if (null? ss)
        best
        (loop (cdr ss)
              (let ((p (car ss)))
                (if (null? (cdr p)) best (max best (- (apply max (cdr p)) (car p)))))))))
(define (longest-run xs)
  (let loop ((ss (suffixes xs)) (best 0))
    (if (null? ss)
        best
        (loop (cdr ss)
              (max best
                   (let walk ((p (car ss)) (n 1))
                     (if (and (pair? (cdr p)) (<= (car p) (cadr p))) (walk (cdr p) (+ n 1)) n)))))))
(display (list 'gain (map max-gain '((7 1 5 3 6 4) (5 4 3) (2 9)))
               'run (map longest-run '((1 2 2 5 1) (9 8 7) (1 2 3 4)))))
(newline)
row-5-emergence.cs-composition:
(define (walk-pairs! f head)
  (pair-fold (lambda (p acc) (f p) (+ acc 1)) 0 head))
(define (compact! head pred)
  (let ((visited (walk-pairs! (lambda (p)
                                (let drop ()
                                  (if (and (pair? (cdr p)) (pred (cadr p)))
                                      (begin (set-cdr! p (cddr p)) (drop)))))
                              head)))
    (list 'kept (cdr head) 'nodes-visited visited 'survivors (length (cdr head)))))
(define a (cons 'anchor (list 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8)))
(define b (cons 'anchor (list 2 4 6)))
(define c (cons 'anchor (list 1 3 5)))
(display (list 'mixed (compact! a even?)
               'all-gone (compact! b even?)
               'untouched (compact! c even?)))
(newline)
row-5-emergence.base: pair-fold hands the callback each successive tail of the list, and saves the cdr first so the callback may splice.
row-5-emergence.emergent: eng: deltas is one pair-fold; alarm-report builds on it to report how many points were seen, which step indices spiked past a threshold, and the worst excursion, so the same reading tape answers a strict and a lenient question. math: suffixes is one pair-fold; max-gain finds the best buy-then-sell over any suffix and longest-run finds the longest non-decreasing stretch starting anywhere, both by asking each suffix a question it can answer alone. cs: walk-pairs! is one pair-fold used purely for its side effect; compact! filters a live list in place through it and reports how many nodes were walked against how many survived, which is the number that shows the walk followed saved cdrs rather than the list's current shape.
row-5-emergence.meta: The cs composition is the honest one: nodes-visited exceeds the survivor count whenever anything was removed, because pair-fold keeps following the cdrs it captured. That is not a defect, it is the mechanism -- and a compaction routine that reported nodes-visited as its length would be wrong in a way nothing else would catch. Every larger function here calls its helper and cannot run without it.
row-5-emergence.eng: A spike report needs both the indices and the magnitude, and both fall out of one difference list. Computing the differences once and asking two questions of them beats two passes over the readings.
row-5-emergence.math: Best gain over a suffix and longest non-decreasing run are both 'ask each suffix' problems, which is why one helper serves both. Each has a linear solution; the suffix version is the specification the linear one has to match.
row-5-emergence.cs: In-place compaction keeps every existing reference to the list valid. Rebuilding does not, and the bug that follows -- one holder still seeing the old contents -- shows up long after the filter ran.
